newsitem.title: UK: UK farmers face testing time lifting sugar beet.
newsitem.headline: UK farmers face testing time lifting sugar beet.

text.p: Sticky ground conditions are hampering British farmers in their efforts to lift sugar beet from this year's harvest and factory deliveries are being delayed due to the larger crop, beet experts said on Friday.
"Harvesting is going very well but conditions are described generally as testing," said an official at British Sugar, adding that this meant the ground was sticky in some key beet areas.
As of December 7, 29 percent of the crop was still in the ground, compared with 25 percent at the same time in 1995/96.

The official added that 24 percent was in store on farms or in clamps by the roadside, compared with 25 percent last year, while 46 percent of beets had already been delivered and processed, after 50 percent at the same stage in 1995/96.

But an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU) voiced concern over the beets which had yet to be lifted due to the larger harvest, as in the past all the crop would normally have been lifted by this stage.

"We've still got this big crop...but the amount (of beet) in the ground is a concern because the recommendation is really to have everything lifted by December 10 to avoid the frosts," the NFU official said.

"If there's a widespread frost, it could wipe out 30 percent of this year's crop -- it's a risk. If it (beet) gets frosted conditions which are quite serious, then it simply can't go into the factory," she said.
The British Sugar official said between five and 10 percent of beets would be left in the ground by Christmas (December 25).
The crop's average sugar content stood at 18.24 percent, up from the 16.74 percent reported for the same stage last year.

Britain is widely expected to turn in a larger sugar production in 1996/97. Trade house Czarnikow, for example, has forecast British output at 1.50 million tonnes raw value this season after 1.33 million in 1995/96.

This year's campaign started late to give beets more chance to develop and take advantage of mild autumn weather. But the late start has meant more risk to the crop as a whole because a higher percentage of beets will still have to be lifted.

Other problems reported have been availability of polypropylene clamp covers to protect beets which have been lifted but must be stored while factories process the larger tonnage, the NFU official said.
Some delays had also been noted in the issuing of delivery permits, the paperwork needed by farmers to hand over the beets to factories.
"It's simply capacity, the factories cannot cope with that level of beet. They're only taking in as much as they can and don't want to store too much," she said.
